## The big idea

A flow meter is Bernoulli wearing a hard hat: **squeeze the flow, read
the pressure drop**, and one honest fudge factor — the discharge
coefficient $C_d$ — pays for everything the ideal equation ignored. The
engineering is in the trade-offs: a sharp orifice is cheap and wasteful,
a venturi is expensive and gentle, and a pitot tube measures a point
instead of the whole pipe.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: β = d/D
The bore-to-pipe ratio. It sets the signal ($\Delta p \sim \beta^{-4}$ish
— small bore, big reading) *and* the permanent loss. Meter sizing is the
art of picking β so the transmitter can read the signal without the pump
paying forever.
:::

1. Why does the ideal meter equation *over*-predict flow, and how is that repaired?
2. What's the difference between the ΔP a meter *reads* and the ΔP the system *loses*?
3. When is a pitot tube the right instrument instead?

## Squeeze and read

Send flow through a smooth contraction from pipe diameter $D$ to throat
diameter $d$. Mass conservation speeds it up; Bernoulli converts the
speed-up into a pressure *drop* between pipe tap and throat tap. Run the
two equations together and solve for flow:

$$Q_\text{ideal} = A_t\,\sqrt{\frac{2\,\Delta p}{\rho}}\;
\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^4}}, \qquad \beta = d/D.$$

The $\sqrt{1-\beta^4}$ factor is Bernoulli's upstream kinetic-energy term
kept honest (the "velocity of approach" correction — drop it and you've
pretended the pipe fluid starts from rest). Reality then under-delivers
relative to this ideal: the jet contracts past a sharp edge (the vena
contracta you met in 4.1), boundary layers thin the throat, a little
friction taxes the trip. Rather than model each sin, industry measures
their combined toll once and bottles it:

$$Q = C_d \, Q_\text{ideal}.$$

For a sharp **orifice plate**, $C_d \approx 0.61$ — the contraction is
severe. For a **venturi**'s guided contraction, $C_d \approx 0.98$ —
nearly ideal. A **flow nozzle** splits the difference at ~0.96. One
number per geometry, tabulated for a century, standardized in ISO 5167;
this is the productive way to be wrong.

## The reading is not the bill

Here is the distinction that separates instrument engineers from
catalog-readers. The $\Delta p$ between the taps is the **signal** — most
of it is speed, and speed can be *slowed back down* into pressure. What
the system permanently loses depends on how gracefully that happens. A
venturi's long diffuser recovers all but ~12% of the reading. An orifice
recovers almost nothing — the jet bursts into a churn of eddies and the
head is gone ($\approx (1-\beta^{1.9})$ of the reading, i.e. most of it).
You will feed `permanent_loss` into Unit 8's head equation as a minor
loss, forever, on every liter.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof meter42 = Inputs.select(["orifice", "venturi", "nozzle"], {value: "orifice", label: "meter type"})
viewof beta42 = Inputs.range([0.3, 0.75], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "β = d/D"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - meter42
#|   - beta42
w = water(20)
D, Q = 0.10, 0.008                       # 100 mm line, 8 L/s design flow
d = beta42 * D
dP = meter_dP(meter42, D, d, Q, w.rho)
loss = permanent_loss(meter42, dP, beta42)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
ax.barh(['ΔP the transmitter reads', 'ΔP the system loses forever'],
        [dP/1000, loss/1000], color=['steelblue', 'crimson'])
for i, v in enumerate([dP, loss]):
    ax.annotate(f' {v/1000:.2f} kPa', (v/1000, i), va='center')
ax.set_xlabel('kPa'); ax.set_xlim(0, max(dP/1000*1.25, 1))
ax.set_title(f"{meter42}, β = {beta42:.2f}, 8 L/s in a 100 mm line "
             f"— loss is {100*loss/dP:.0f}% of the reading")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Two sweeps to run. **Shrink β** on the orifice: the signal balloons
(great for a cheap transmitter) and so does the bill. **Switch to the
venturi at the same β**: nearly the same signal, a tenth the bill — which
is why venturis guard the big permanent lines and orifice plates get the
utility taps. The sizing problem runs backwards too — given a
transmitter's range, `size_meter` finds the bore. That's the instrument
engineer's daily bread, and homework will serve it.

**The pitot tube** answers a different question. Point a tube into the
flow; the fluid entering it stops (a *stagnation point*), converting its
velocity head into extra pressure. Read stagnation minus static and
invert: $U = \sqrt{2\Delta p/\rho}$ — a **point** velocity, not a pipe
average. It's the airspeed indicator on every aircraft (and the thing
whose icing has caused real crashes — a blunt fact worth carrying), and
in the lab it's how you traverse a duct to map a profile… which you then
read with your 6.2 eyes.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
The meter's ΔP reading is **not** the price of the measurement. The
reading is mostly recoverable speed; the *permanent* loss is what the
diffuser fails to reclaim. Confusing them makes the venturi look
pointless (same reading!) and the orifice look free (it isn't — you pay
its toll on every liter for the life of the plant).
:::

## Earn it — 2 quick gates

Two gates on the two numbers every obstruction meter lives by: the reading, and the bill. Ungraded; hints after a miss; **Show me** after two. Arguing about a gate with a classmate is the assignment, not a violation.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Your orifice ΔP reading rises from 8 kPa to 32 kPa. Flow rate rose by a factor of…?"
     data-answer="2.0" data-tol="0.02" data-units="×"
     data-hint="Q ∝ √ΔP — the ½ρV² heart of the meter. Four times the signal is twice the flow."
     data-solution="√(32/8) = 2.0×. The square root is also why turndown haunts orifice meters: 10:1 in flow is 100:1 in signal."
     data-target="fme-s2"></div>
```

::: {#fme-s2 .fl-hidden}
The reading is the signal. The *permanent loss* is what the pump pays forever — and it depends on the geometry downstream:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="A venturi (β ≈ 0.5) keeps ~12% of its reading as permanent loss. At a 20 kPa reading, the everlasting bill is…?"
     data-answer="2.4" data-tol="0.03" data-units="kPa"
     data-hint="12% of 20. The point is not the arithmetic — it is that an orifice at the same reading keeps ~55%."
     data-solution="0.12 × 20 = 2.4 kPa forever, vs ~11 kPa for an orifice showing the same signal. The diffuser is the difference."></div>
```

Signal scales with √, rent scales with geometry — pick meters with both numbers on the table.

:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** Why does $C_d$ for an orifice (0.61) sit so close to the vena-contracta area ratio, while a venturi's sits near 1?</summary>
The orifice's dominant "sin" *is* the contraction — the jet necks down to
~60% of the bore area, so the ideal equation overcounts area by exactly
that. The venturi's guided walls prevent the contraction, leaving only
minor friction to apologize for.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Your orifice reads ΔP = 25 kPa at design flow. Flow drops to half. What does it read now?</summary>
About 6.2 kPa — the reading scales with $Q^2$. This quadratic squash is
the DP meter's real weakness: at 25% flow the signal is 1/16th of range,
drowning in transmitter noise. ("Turndown ratio" is the catalog word.)
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** A pitot tube in the center of a pipe reads a velocity of 2.0 m/s in fully turbulent flow. Is $Q$ = 2.0 × (pipe area) an over- or under-estimate, and roughly by how much?</summary>
Over — the centerline is the profile's fastest point. For turbulent flow
the average is ~0.8–0.85 of centerline (blunt profile), so ~15–20% high.
For laminar flow you'd be 100% high (center = 2× average): the regime
changes the correction. Everything connects.
</details>

## Bring to class

Your plant has one transmitter model (range 0–30 kPa) and a 100 mm water
line at 8 L/s. Come with a defensible choice — meter type and β — and the
one-sentence bill your choice sends to the pump.
